• Spider 2.0[ 46]: a next-generation evaluation framework of 632 real-world enterprise workflow problems that extends the canonical Spider task toend-to-end problem solvingover relational databases. Tasks are drawn from enterprise-scale databases hosted on cloud and local systems (e.g., BigQuery, Snowflake, SQLite), frequently involve schemas with more than a thousand columns, and may require multiple SQL dialects, project-level codebases, and lengthy queries. Spider 2.0 is designed to reflect realistic analytical workflows: it evaluates not only single-shot NL→SQL parsers but also multi-stage pipelines and autonomous agents that inspect schemas, issue exploratory queries, validate execution, and repair errors. Two derived settings,Spider 2.0-Lite andSpider 2.0-Snow, isolate the pure Text-to-SQL component.

Key characteristics that distinguish Spider 2.0 from earlier benchmarks include: – Execution-centric evaluation.Scoring is based on whether the produced results are correct when executed against the target databases, which allows single-shot parsers, prompt-based LLMs, and multi-stage agentic systems to be compared on a common footing rather than by surface-form matching. – Multi-stage workflows.Many tasks require multi-step interaction: inspecting the schema, issuing partial queries, examining intermediate results, and performing repair or validation steps. This exposes failure modes that single-shot benchmarks cannot capture. 6

results.text: • BIRD[ 47] (BIg Bench for laRge-scale Database-grounded Text-to-SQL evaluation): a crossdomain benchmark designed to stress-test models on large, heterogeneous schemas and substantial data volumes. Here,cross-domainrefers to coverage of a wide variety of professional fields and database schemas, ranging from sports and finance to healthcare, blockchain, and education, so that evaluation is not biased toward any single domain. BIRD comprises 12,751 unique question–SQL pairs over 95 real-world databases totaling 33.4 GB of relational data, spanning 37 professional domains, and evaluates parser robustness against schema complexity, data scale, and domain variability. • UNITE[ 44] (A Unified Benchmark for Text-to-SQL Evaluation): UNITE assembles and normalizes eighteen public Text-to-SQL datasets into a single unified format to evaluate generalization across diverse schemas, SQL patterns, and domains.

ReViSQL (UIUC, March 2026).ReViSQL [100] is the first method to report human-level accuracy on BIRD, reaching 93.2% execution accuracy on an expert-verified BIRD Mini-Dev split and narrowly exceeding the 92.96% human-expert reference reported by the original benchmark. The paper’s central claim is methodological rather than architectural: it argues that the remaining gap between state-of-the-art agents and humans is driven by training-data quality rather than reasoning-pipeline design. To support this claim, the authors constructBIRD-Verified, a 2.5K-instance subset of the BIRD training set corrected through two to four rounds of independent review by SQL experts. They report annotation errors in 61.1% of the audited instances (52.1% in gold SQL queries, 26.2% in natural language questions, and 18.2% in external-knowledge fields), which is broadly consistent with concurrent findings on benchmark unreliability [39, 40].

results.text: 4.3 Evaluating Robustness via SQL2NL: Schema-Aligned Paraphrasing The SQL2NL framework [69] proposes a schema-aware approach to measure and improve therobustness of NL-to-SQL systems under lexical and syntactic variation. Rather than paraphrasing natural language questions naïvely (which can inadvertently change schema links), SQL2NL generates paraphrases conditioned on thegold SQLand the target database schema, producing diverse utterances that preserve the original intent while keeping schema alignment intact. This makes it possible to measure how sensitive a model is to wording, independently of schema-linking errors.

results.text: Methodology.SQL2NL (i) ingests a gold SQL query and its schema description; (ii) prompts a generation model with constraints that encourage lexical and syntactic diversity while forbidding schemaidentifier leakage; (iii) validates paraphrase fidelity through automatic embedding-based checks and targeted human review of a sample; and (iv) evaluates NL-to-SQL systems by comparing execution accuracy on the original questions with that on the SQL2NL paraphrases. The framework supports weighted (human-adjusted) scoring so that low-quality paraphrases do not unduly penalize systems. SQL2NL can also produce augmented training data for robustness-oriented fine-tuning. Evaluation protocol and datasets.The authors apply SQL2NL to Spider and BIRD and stratify their analyses by query complexity (number of joins, nested clauses, and aggregates). The primary metrics are execution accuracyand therobustness gap, defined as the drop in execution accuracy from the original to the paraphrased questions.

A further, and often overlooked, threat to validity is the quality of the benchmarks themselves: recent expert audits report annotation errors in more than half of the examined instances of BIRD Mini-Dev and Spider 2.0-Snow, enough to change both reported accuracies and leaderboard rankings [ 39, 40]. Recent work therefore increasingly favors hybrid evaluation protocols in which the semantics of the generated SQL are measured alongside syntactic faithfulness and latency, and progress in agentic methods has motivated metrics that account for tool usage and multi-step behavior. 14
